com.dravensoft.arena.job: invite and convert: marketing, commerce, onboarding, pricing, a landing page somebody arrives on

r-surface.$description:
A product card is a thing you want to touch, so its corner is softer than a panel
you want to read. One step up the scale rather than an invented number, which is the rule an
extension holds to everywhere: it re-values a role, and the value it moves to is still Arena's.

r-surface-floating.$description:
The floating tier moves with the surface tier and stays one step below it, so a menu
still reads as lighter than the card it opens over. Moving one without the other is the
half-applied look the two roles exist to prevent.

r-control.$description:
A softer button. Not a pill: a pill reads as a tag or a filter chip, and a call to
action that looks like a filter is a call to action nobody presses.

r-control-sm.$description:
A checkbox box and a segment move with the buttons, one step below them, which is
the relationship roles.json authored and not a second decision taken here. Left behind, a 4px
checkbox beside a 10px button reads as a control the extension forgot rather than as a small
one, and it is the same half-applied look r-surface-floating exists to prevent one tier up.

r-field.$description:
Fields follow controls, because a form reads as one object when its inputs and its
submit button share a corner.

r-marker.$description:
A price badge sits on a rounder card, so a square-cornered marker would read as
stuck on rather than part of it.

bw-surface.$description:
The change this extension is actually about. Arena groups by drawing the region,
which is cheap in pixels and right for dense data; here the grouping is carried by elevation
and air instead, which is the Gestalt trade between common region and figure/ground.

Safe to remove because a surface is not a user interface component: WCAG 1.4.11 asks 3:1 of a
CONTROL's boundary and of a meaningful graphic, and a card is neither. bw-control and bw-field
are therefore untouched below, and bw-separator with them, because a table that lost the rules
between its rows when its frame went would stop being readable.

shadow-surface-rest.$description:
What replaces the border in DARK, and the reason this extension varies with the
theme at all. A drop shadow is a darkening, so it separates a light card from a light page and
does almost nothing between a dark card and a dark page.

The obvious alternative was measured and refused: moving the card onto a different step of the
surface scale. The widest step Dravensoft's base ramp offers in dark is base-300 on base-100 at
1.13:1, and neutral on base-100 at 1.22:1. Neither is an edge anybody sees, and the ramp belongs
to the consumer, so an extension cannot widen it.

A rim light inverts the direction instead. White at 12% over base-200 reads about 1.5:1 against
the page, because it is light on dark rather than dark on dark. It is inset along the top edge
and not a ring, which matters: a ring would be a hairline drawn around a region, which is the
mechanism this extension traded away. An edge lit from above is a statement about an object
standing in light, so it is still figure and ground.

In light a darkening is a boundary again, so the ordinary drop shadow is the
answer and it REPLACES the rim rather than joining it: two depth cues on one edge read as a
seam. The lightest step of the elevation scale, because a page of product cards each carrying a
dialog's depth reads as a pile rather than a grid.

shadow-control-raised.$description:
A call to action that lifts further than anything else on the page. This is where
a voice whose job is to invite and convert spends most of its emphasis, and it is spent on one
element per view, which is the same rule as one primary accent per view.

lift-control.$description:
Two pixels, and no more: the travel has to read as an answer to the pointer rather
than as the layout moving. It is a length rather than an alias because the base value is 0 and
there is no scale step for a distance a control travels.

pad-surface.$description:
20px to 32px, which is the other half of the air this voice spends. Ground around
a figure and room inside it are one decision made twice: a card given more space on the page and
none inside it reads as a crowded object standing alone, which is worse than either.

The floating tier is untouched, and that is the point of the split: a dialog roomed up by the
same ratio would start pushing its own buttons past the fold.

rhythm-component.$description:
The ground a figure needs around it. This voice took the line off a surface and
asked elevation and air to carry the grouping, and air is half of that sentence: a card with no
border and no room around it reads as a stripe of a longer surface rather than as an object.

rhythm-group is deliberately left alone. The air INSIDE a group is what makes a label and its
field read as one thing, and widening it would loosen the figure while the ground grew, which is
the opposite of what figure and ground means.

rhythm-section.$description:
Section air grows further than component air, so the ladder stays a ladder: group
is 12, component becomes 24 and section becomes 40, which reads 1 to 2 to 3.3 where the default
reads 1 to 1.33 to 2. A voice that widened one step without the other would flatten the very
hierarchy the steps exist to state.

dur-hover.$description:
Slower than Arena's default, which is the whole difference between an interface
that acknowledges a pointer and one that responds to it. Still inside the transition range, so
nothing here becomes motion a person waits on.

ease-hover.$description:
The other half of the same decision, and the half a duration cannot make. Arena's
default curve leaves at full speed and settles, which is an interface answering the instant the
pointer lands. This one starts from rest, which is what a thing with mass does: 220ms on that
curve reads as an object being moved, where 220ms on the default reads as the same instant answer
taking longer than it should.

Derived from the principle rather than chosen beside it. A figure standing off a ground is an
OBJECT, and an object has inertia; a voice that grouped by drawing a region has nothing to give
mass to, which is why the default curve is right there and wrong here. Still one of Arena's three
steps, because the value a role moves to is the language's and not the voice's.

press-scale.$description:
0.98 to 0.96, which is the return trip of the two pixels lift-control spends. A
control that rises under the pointer and then sinks under the press has completed a gesture; one
that rises and then barely moves has started one.

Twice the default and no further. Past about 0.95 a button reads as a soft thing being squashed
rather than a solid one being pressed, and this voice is about objects standing on a floor rather
than about toys.

fs-h1.$description:
A page heading that carries a page rather than titling a panel. The base ladder
accelerates gently because a console has many peers on screen at once; a landing has few, so the
jump from the body it sits over is wider here.

The reading sizes below h2 do not move, in this extension or in any other. Body and chrome text
is the one thing every voice shares, because how large a paragraph is set is a legibility
decision and not an expressive one. An extension widens the hierarchy by raising what shouts,
never by shrinking what is read.

fs-display.$description:
The step a hero headline is set at. 80 over 64 is a fifth again, which reads as a
different kind of page rather than as the same page with bigger type.

fs-hero.$description:
The largest step anything is actually set at, and the reason fs-hero was kept when
it had no consumer.
